pages.title: How do many electrons share an atom?

blocks.text: An atom can contain many electrons, but they cannot all occupy the same lowest state. We need rules combining orbital energies with restrictions on electron states.
An electronic configuration records occupation, such as 1s²2s²2p⁶. Superscripts count electrons; they are not orbital charges.
In 1s², the 1 is n, s identifies l=0, and the superscript 2 is the electron count in that subshell. Writing 1s² does not locate two electrons at fixed points; it specifies occupied quantum states.

pages.transition: Read the configuration notation before using it to distribute electrons.

pages.title: Compare hydrogen and multi-electron energies

blocks.text: Hydrogen-like orbitals with the same n have equal energy in the basic model. In multi-electron atoms, electron repulsion and shielding make energy depend on n and l.

Shielding means inner electrons reduce nuclear attraction experienced by outer ones. Penetration describes how effectively orbital density reaches near the nucleus. For one shell, s penetrates more than p, then d and f.

Penetration and shielding work together. An s electron samples regions closer to the nucleus more effectively than a p electron of the same shell, so it can experience greater effective attraction and lower energy. This explains why multi-electron 2s and 2p orbitals need not be degenerate.

pages.transition: Orbital-energy differences tell us where filling begins.

pages.title: Use the energy-order guide

blocks.text: The Aufbau principle fills available lower-energy orbitals first. The n+l rule places smaller n+l first; on a tie, smaller n first. It gives 1s, 2s, 2p, 3s, 3p, 4s, 3d, 4p,… .
For 4s, n+l=4; for 3d, n+l=5, so 4s starts first in the simple filling order. Energies change with occupation; this is a ground-state guide, not one fixed ladder for every atom and ion.

Compare 3d and 4p: both have n+l=5, so the smaller n wins and 3d fills before 4p in the simple rule. Compare 4p and 5s: both have n+l=5, so 4p precedes 5s. These ties show why n+l alone is not the complete ordering rule.

pages.transition: The energy guide must be combined with restrictions on allowed states.

pages.title: Apply Pauli’s exclusion principle

blocks.text: No two electrons in an atom can share all four quantum numbers. A single orbital therefore accommodates at most two electrons, and their spins must be opposite.
An orbital box may contain↑↓, never↑↑. This limits s, p, d, f subshells to 2, 6, 10, 14 electrons respectively because they contain 1, 3, 5, 7 orbitals.

A p subshell has three orbitals, each holding at most two electrons, so its capacity is 3×2=6. A d subshell has five, so its capacity is 10. Occupation notation such as 2p⁷ violates capacity before any detailed energy calculation is attempted.

pages.transition: Within equal-energy orbitals, decide whether electrons should pair.

pages.title: Apply Hund’s rule before pairing

blocks.text: Within degenerate orbitals, electrons occupy different orbitals singly with parallel spins before pairing. Degenerate means equal in energy, such as the three p orbitals of a free atom.
Nitrogen’s 2p³ arrangement is↑,↑,↑ across three boxes, not↑↓,↑, empty. Hund’s rule avoids premature pairing and describes the lower-energy ground-state arrangement.

For carbon, Z=6 gives 1s²2s²2p². Put the two p electrons in different p orbitals with parallel spins:↑,↑, empty. Pairing them in one box would obey the two-electron limit but violate the ground-state Hund arrangement. Pauli and Hund answer different checks.

pages.transition: Use all three rules on a concrete atom.

pages.title: Build oxygen’s configuration

blocks.text: Oxygen has Z=8, so a neutral atom has eight electrons. Fill 1s², then 2s², leaving four electrons in 2p: 1s²2s²2p⁴. The superscripts total 2+2+4=8.

Place three 2p electrons separately, then pair the fourth with opposite spin in one box. Two electrons remain unpaired. Counting the electrons checks the configuration; applying Hund checks the arrangement.

For nitrogen, 1s²2s²2p³ gives three unpaired electrons. Adding one electron to obtain oxygen produces 2p⁴ and two unpaired electrons; continuing to fluorine 2p⁵ leaves one, and neon 2p⁶ leaves zero. The sequence follows separate occupation before pairing.

pages.transition: A noble-gas core makes longer configurations easier to check.

pages.title: Use a noble-gas core correctly

blocks.text: Sodium’s eleven-electron configuration is 1s²2s²2p⁶3s¹. Its first ten electrons match neon, so write[Ne]3s¹. Chlorine’s seventeen electrons give[Ne]3s²3p⁵.
The bracket represents an entire filled inner configuration, not one electron. Add core electrons to the written outer superscripts when checking total electron count.

For Z=20, fill to argon’s eighteen-electron core, then 4s²: calcium is[Ar]4s². The full superscript sum is 20. The highest occupied shell is n=4 even though a 3d subshell also exists as an allowed set of orbitals; existence does not mean occupation.

pages.transition: Compare the simple filling prediction with observed near-degenerate exceptions.

pages.title: Recognise chromium and copper exceptions

blocks.text: Chromium’s observed ground state is[Ar]3d⁵4s¹ rather than the naive[Ar]3d⁴4s². Copper is[Ar]3d¹⁰4s¹ rather than[Ar]3d⁹4s².

The competing energies are close. Half-filled and filled subshells gain stabilisation associated with symmetric distribution and exchange effects. Actual total energy, not a blindly followed diagram, selects the ground state.

Count chromium explicitly: argon contributes 18, 3d⁵ contributes 5 and 4s¹ contributes 1, totalling 24. Copper similarly gives 18+10+1=29. The exception changes distribution between close-energy subshells, not the required total number of electrons.

pages.transition: Explain why certain occupations gain additional stabilisation.

pages.title: Explain subshell stability carefully

blocks.text: Exchange stabilisation is associated with parallel-spin electrons in degenerate orbitals. More possible exchanges contribute to the stability of particular occupations, alongside other electron interactions.

In 3d⁵, five d orbitals are singly occupied with parallel spins; in 3d¹⁰ they are filled. Do not predict electron promotion for every possible half-filled subshell: the complete energy balance decides.

For five parallel-spin electrons in five d orbitals, there are 5×4/2=10 distinct pairs that can exchange in the elementary counting argument. This illustrates the many possible exchange relationships in a half-filled set; it does not by itself calculate the total atomic energy.

Do not confuse a half-filled shell with a half-filled subshell. Nitrogen has half-filled 2p³, but its n=2 shell also contains 2s². Chromium’s half-filled 3d⁵ likewise refers to the d subshell rather than all orbitals with n=3.

pages.transition: Finish by checking electron count, energy order and spin occupation together.

blocks.text: Use the energy-order guide, Pauli’s two-electron restriction and Hund’s single-occupation rule together. Check electron total before interpreting the configuration.
Observed exceptions show why total energy matters. The resulting repeated valence-electron patterns will explain chemical families in the next chapter.

questions.question: Why can one orbital hold at most two electrons?
questions.answer: Pauli forbids identical sets of four quantum numbers; the pair must differ in spin.

questions.question: How do three p electrons occupy degenerate orbitals?
questions.answer: Singly in separate orbitals with parallel spins before pairing.

questions.question: Write magnesium’s configuration, Z=12.
questions.answer: [Ne]3s², with ten core electrons and two valence electrons.

questions.question: Which fills first by n+l: 4s or 3d?
questions.answer: 4s has n+l=4, while 3d has 5; the simple filling order begins 4s first.

questions.question: How many unpaired electrons has oxygen?
questions.answer: Two, from the Hund arrangement of 2p⁴.

questions.question: Does[Ne] stand for one electron?
questions.answer: No. It denotes neon’s filled ten-electron core.
